ai.literal: If one asks what virtuous action is, it is non-killing; killing will bring all other actions.
ai.translation: If you ask what virtuous action is, it is non-killing; killing will bring about all other harmful deeds.
ai.modern: அறச்செயல் எது என்று கேட்டால் அது கொல்லாமையே ஆகும்; உயிரைக் கொல்லுதல் மற்ற தீய செயல்கள் அனைத்தையும் கொண்டுவந்து சேர்க்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the essence of virtue as the practice of non-killing. The author states that if one inquires about the foremost virtuous deed, the answer is simply not taking any life. On the other hand, committing the act of killing is described as a gateway sin that brings about all other harmful and evil deeds. By upholding non-killing, a person is naturally protected from falling into other vices.

ai.literal: Sharing and eating, protecting many lives, among all those compiled by scholars, is the foremost.
ai.translation: Sharing one's food with others and protecting all living beings is the foremost virtue among all those compiled by scholars in their scriptures.
ai.modern: உணவைப் பகிர்ந்து உண்டு, பல உயிர்களையும் காப்பாற்றுவது, அறநூல்களை எழுதியவர்கள் தொகுத்துக் கூறிய அறங்கள் எல்லாவற்றிலும் முதன்மையானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the pinnacle of virtue as the active protection of life. The poet states that sharing what one has with other living beings (paguttuṇṭu) and safeguarding them from harm (ōmputhal) is the greatest moral duty. While scholars of scriptures have compiled and classified numerous virtues, this practice of compassion and non-injury stands above them all. The term 'nūlōr' refers to the wise authors of ethical texts, and 'talai' establishes this specific path of sharing and protecting as the supreme crown of their teachings.

ai.literal: As the single foremost good thing is non-killing; next, following behind that, non-lying is good.
ai.translation: Non-killing is the single foremost virtue; next to it, following closely behind, is the virtue of truthfulness.
ai.modern: ஒப்பற்ற ஒரு நன்மையாக விளங்குவது கொல்லாமை ஆகும்; அதற்கு அடுத்தபடியாக, அதனைச் சார்ந்து விளங்கும் பொய்யாமை நல்லதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two of the greatest ethical virtues: non-killing and truthfulness. It establishes non-killing as the absolute, singular foremost virtue in life. Immediately following it, as the next best virtue that supports or accompanies it, is truthfulness. By using the phrase 'pin caara' (to follow behind), the poet shows that while truthfulness is highly virtuous, it stands second to the supreme virtue of preserving life.

ai.literal: The good path that which is called if you ask what, it is the path that embraces the non-killing of any single thing.
ai.translation: If you ask what is called the good path, it is the path that embraces the non-killing of any living thing whatsoever.
ai.modern: நல்ல வழி என்று சொல்லப்படுவது எதுவென்றால், எந்த ஒரு உயிரையும் கொல்லாத அறவழியைப் பின்பற்றுவதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the ultimate path of virtue by posing a direct question and answering it. The 'good path' (nallāṟu) is identified as the path of non-killing (kollāmai). The phrase 'yātonṟum' emphasizes that this applies to absolutely any living creature, without exception. The word 'sūḻum' suggests actively embracing, protecting, or constantly pursuing this principle, showing that true virtue lies in the conscious preservation of all life.

ai.literal: Worldly existence fearing, among those who renounced all, killing fearing, non-killing he who cherishes, is foremost.
ai.translation: Among all those who have renounced the world out of fear for the instability of worldly existence, he who cherishes non-killing out of fear for taking life is the foremost.
ai.modern: வாழ்க்கை நிலைக்கு அஞ்சி உலகத்தைத் துறந்தவர்கள் எல்லாரிலும், கொலை செய்ய அஞ்சிக் கொல்லாமையைக் கடைப்பிடிப்பவன் முதன்மையானவன் ஆவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two types of fear and renunciation to establish the supremacy of non-killing. Some people renounce worldly life because they fear its instability and suffering. However, the poet declares that the person who fears the act of killing and actively practices non-killing is the greatest among all ascetics. This emphasizes that compassion towards other living beings is a higher spiritual virtue than merely seeking one's own escape from worldly troubles.

ai.literal: Upon the lifetime of one who conducts himself having undertaken non-killing, Death who consumes life will not advance.
ai.translation: Death, who devours lives, will not advance against the lifetime of one who adopts and practices non-killing.
ai.modern: கொல்லாமையைத் தன் விரதமாக ஏற்றுக்கொண்டு வாழ்கின்றவனுடைய வாழ்நாளின் மேல், உயிரைக் குடிக்கின்ற எமனானவன் செல்ல மாட்டான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme virtue of non-killing by stating that even Death, who normally devours all lives, will not cut short the life of one who practices non-killing. The word 'கூற்று' refers to Death, the divider of life, and 'உயிருண்ணும்' describes Death's nature as a consumer of life. By saying Death 'will not advance' (செல்லாது) against such a person's lifetime (வாழ்நாள்மேல்), the poet emphasizes that a life of harmlessness naturally commands longevity and protection from untimely demise.

ai.literal: One's own life even if departing, do not do oneself another's sweet life removing action.
ai.translation: Even if one were to lose one's own life, one should never perform an action that takes away the sweet life of another being.
ai.modern: தன் உயிர் உடலை விட்டுப் பிரிவதாக இருந்தாலும், ஒருவன் மற்றொரு உயிரினத்தின் இனிய உயிரைப் போக்கும் செயலைச் செய்யக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes the absolute and uncompromising nature of non-violence. It instructs that even if one's own life is at stake, one must not perform any action that destroys the life of another creature. The term 'இன்னுயிர்' (sweet life) emphasizes that existence is precious and dear to every living being. By prioritizing the life of others over one's own survival, the text sets an ultimate standard of compassion.

ai.literal: Even if the wealth that yields good is great, to the noble, the wealth obtained by killing is the lowest.
ai.translation: Even if the wealth that brings goodness is immensely great, to the virtuous, wealth obtained by killing other living beings is utterly base.
ai.modern: நன்மையைத் தரும் செல்வம் மிகப் பெரியதாக இருந்தாலும், பிற உயிர்களைக் கொல்வதன் மூலம் கிடைக்கும் செல்வம் சான்றோர்களுக்கு மிக இழிவானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the absolute commitment of virtuous people to the principle of non-killing. Even if a particular gain or wealth ('ஆக்கம்') is incredibly vast ('பெரிது') and promises great benefits ('நன்றாகும்'), it is deemed utterly base ('கடை') by the noble ('சான்றோர்') if it is acquired by destroying life ('கொன்று'). For the truly wise, no amount of material prosperity can justify the act of killing. The contrast between the greatness of the gain and its moral lowliness emphasizes that ethical purity always triumphs over material success.

ai.literal: Those of killing-occupation who are undiscerning people, vile-occupation-holders they are, in the mind of those who discern baseness.
ai.translation: In the estimation of those who discern the baseness of slaughter, people whose occupation is killing are regarded as doers of the vilest deeds.
ai.modern: கொலை செய்வதன் இழிவை உணர்ந்தவர்களின் மனதில், கொலையைத் தொழிலாகக் கொண்ட மனிதர்கள் இழிவான செயலைச் செய்பவர்களாகவே கருதப்படுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how those who kill are perceived by wise and compassionate people. The word 'mākkaḷ' refers to humans who lack higher moral discernment and act on animal instincts. To those who truly understand the inherent baseness ('punmai') of taking a life, anyone engaged in the profession of killing ('kolaivinaiyar') is seen as performing the lowest, most degraded deeds ('pulaivinaiyar'). The verse emphasizes that true social and moral standing is determined by one's compassion, not by outward human form.

ai.literal: Those who separated life from the body, they say, are those who have a life of unending misery with a diseased body.
ai.translation: Wise people say that those who live a life of unending misery in a diseased and suffering body are those who once separated life from another's body.
ai.modern: உடம்பிலிருந்து உயிரைப் பிரித்தவர்கள் (கொலை செய்தவர்கள்) என்று, நோயால் துன்புறும் உடம்போடு நீங்காத துன்ப வாழ்க்கையை வாழ்பவர்களை அறிவுடையோர் கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet links the act of killing to the physical suffering experienced in a subsequent existence. The poet suggests that those who suffer from chronic, painful diseases and live a life of unending misery (cellā tī vāḻkkai) in a defective body (ceyiṟ uṭampu) are reaping the consequences of having taken another life. The word 'ceyiṟ' means defect or disease, highlighting physical suffering, while 'cellā tī' represents unceasing, fire-like misery. Through this, the chapter on non-killing (kollāmai) emphasizes that the violence inflicted on others ultimately returns to the perpetrator as physical and mental torment.
